item.title: Even second graders can reason like scientists—if we ask them the right way
item.description: When a child asks "Why does a blowfish puff up?" we often jump in with facts. But what if we paused and suggested that they ask instead, "How does a blowfish puff up?" It may seem like splitting hairs, but this small shift in phrasing could help reshape future generations' capacity for reasoning and critical thought in science and beyond. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nanoscale multiferroic materials open the path to efficient magnetic memory technology
item.description: With the rapid spread of cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data centers, global energy consumption is rising to new heights. A promising way to reduce this burden is to develop memory devices that store information magnetically yet are written using electric fields. Magnetic memories are nonvolatile, meaning stored information is retained without a power supply. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Predictive tools can confuse rare mutations with dangerous ones
item.description: When a patient's DNA is read, it is compared with a reference version of the human genome. This allows geneticists and rare disease experts to look at a list of places where the patient's DNA differs. Most variations will be harmless and shared with millions of other people, but some can cause illness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beyond the 'Great Divide': What we really know about political polarization
item.description: Americans are deeply divided. At least that's what we've been told for years. But how divided are we really? A new review suggests the answer may depend on how researchers ask the question. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ig Nobel Prize winners reveal why babies smell better than teenagers
item.description: Babies smell wonderful—at least to their parents. An international research team of Ilona Croy, Tomasz Frackowiak, Thomas Hummel and Agnieszka Sorokowska investigated why teenagers lose this special olfactory advantage and has now been awarded an Ig Nobel Prize for the research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Traces of nearly 4 million coins reveal how Rome achieved economic integration
item.description: For centuries, the study of ancient history relied primarily on interpreting classical texts and examining inscriptions and archaeological remains at their sites of origin or in museums. In recent years, however, a little-known transformation has profoundly changed this landscape. The digitization of extensive archaeological collections, coupled with the development of quantitative methods that can integrate millions of scattered records, is ushering in a new era of historical research. Like other scientific disciplines that have benefited from processing colossal amounts of information… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Green thumb' molecule helps leaf stalks grow in crowded conditions
item.description: Potassium (K) is one of the three essential nutrients for plants. It plays a critical role in a wide range of processes, including cell growth, photosynthesis and regulation of water balance. Plants take up K from the soil and circulate it throughout their bodies via molecules called K+ channels. The function of one such K+ channel (called AKT5) in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana has remained a mystery, despite more than 30 years of study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A molecular brake that keeps muscle architecture in check
item.description: Every movement we make, from blinking to sprinting, depends on the ability of muscle fibers to contract in a rapid and coordinated way. Achieving this precision requires an intricate internal membrane network known as the transverse tubule, or T-tubule, system. These narrow membrane invaginations carry electrical signals from the cell surface deep into the muscle fiber, where they trigger the release of calcium needed for contraction. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a plant's refusal to self-pollinate could help India grow more of its own cooking oil
item.description: Most people assume plants reproduce through whatever pollen happens to land on them. This is not true. A collaborative research initiative involving the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN) has mapped and functionally tested the genes that control a natural "self-rejection" system in two widely grown Indian oilseed crops, Brassica rapa (mustard) varieties toria and yellow sarson. This system governs the molecular "lock-and-key" mechanism in certain mustard plants that allows them to reject their own pollen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hot subdwarfs come into focus as AI scans thousands of stars in Gaia data
item.description: There are myriad ways of "being a star," and scientists spend years trying to uncover and understand them. One unusual type is the so-called hot subdwarf—small stars that burn mysteriously hot for their size. Scientists from the Faculty of Physics and the Faculty of Mathematics and Informatics at Vilnius University (VU) are working to explain this strange phenomenon and recently made important breakthroughs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Perseverance rover watches Earth vanish behind Martian moon
item.description: Earth and the Martian moon Phobos dance together in a series of images recently acquired by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover. Earth appears as a point of light in the Martian sky, disappearing behind the crescent of Phobos, the larger of Mars' two moons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Power of disorder' tames CF₄, a semiconductor greenhouse gas that can persist for 50,000 years
item.description: Among the gases used in semiconductor manufacturing, tetrafluoromethane (CF₄) is a greenhouse gas more than 6,000 times as potent as carbon dioxide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Empty nest' can trigger loneliness and loss in older parents, study finds
item.description: Older parents can experience loneliness, emotional distress and a loss of purpose when their children leave home, according to a new pilot study by the University of Hertfordshire. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctic expedition reveals why Southern Ocean clouds remain one of climate science's greatest challenges
item.description: The Southern Ocean plays a pivotal role in regulating Earth's climate, yet the clouds that blanket this remote region remain among the least understood features in atmospheric science. By controlling both incoming sunlight and outgoing heat, these clouds strongly influence Earth's energy balance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists studying cockroach milk and nose-blowing win Ig Nobel prizes
item.description: Ten research teams were honoured on Thursday at a satirical science awards ceremony that was hosted outside the US for the first time due to travel concerns. Researchers who studied milk from cockroaches and analysed soil health using underwear received Ig Nobel prizes celebrating unusual and imaginative contributions to science. The awards organised by a digital magazine called the Annals of Improbable Research shifted to Europe after 35 years in the US over concerns about attendees being able... Publicado también por: Phys.org. Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Early mammals weren't all loners—some may have lived in pairs alongside the dinosaurs
item.description: About 200 million years ago, furry, little egg-laying creatures evolved the ability to feed their offspring with a secretion from special glands: milk. Their evolutionary journey continued, and by about 160 million years ago, the first mammals with a real placenta had come into being. Instead of laying eggs, they gave birth to live young that had been connected directly to their mother via a placenta during pregnancy, allowing the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rapid simulation of heat propagation through multiple rods
item.description: There is an elegant mathematical equation behind many different natural phenomena. From the fractal pattern of a romanesco cauliflower sitting on a grocery store shelf to the flow of rivers, they all have underlying mathematical properties. The way heat propagates from one object to another also has a strikingly complex mathematical basis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Photo: NASA's Hubble spies superbubble scene
item.description: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista in the Large Magellanic Cloud, or LMC, the largest of the small galaxies that orbit our Milky Way galaxy. At just 160,000 light-years away, the LMC offers a close look at highly active star-forming sites like the one in this image. This photogenic nebula, named LHA 120-N44, or N44, is in the constellation Dorado. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chimpanzees have accents too, study finds
item.description: A study has found that young chimpanzees develop distinct population-specific vocal patterns as they mature (ontogeny), challenging the long-held assumption that their calls are inflexible and determined solely by genetics. The work is published in the journal PLOS One. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Malaysia starts cloud seeding to help clear toxic haze
item.description: Malaysia launched a three-day cloud-seeding operation Thursday in a bid to ease hazardous haze choking Sarawak state, as smoke from Indonesian forest fires pushed air quality to dangerous levels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly discovered 1666 manuscript may trace four-lens telescope experiments to Galileo
item.description: A potentially history-altering finding by a University of Limerick researcher may provide the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope demonstrably made by the famous astronomer and scientist Galileo Galilei. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why purpose doesn't always pay: The career cost of workplace climate activism
item.description: Employees advocating for climate action are most likely to be rewarded when their efforts support business goals, while purpose-led activism often goes unrecognized Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wrinkled or smooth? Cell growth mechanics determine shape of plant organs
item.description: When inner and outer cell layers of sepals—the leaf-like plant organs that cover and protect the flower bud before it opens—all grow upward, the organs stay smooth and uniformly stiff, which is optimal for the plant, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite images show how penguins' diets are changing in response to Antarctic climate change
item.description: The color of penguin poop, as seen from space, is offering a new window into how Antarctica's ecology and environment are changing over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scottish 'pregnant grandmother' microbe bursts open after growing offspring within
item.description: Scientists have revealed a bizarre microscopic creature that reproduces in a way reminiscent of the horror film" Alien." The microbe grows one or more new cells inside its own body before the outer "mother" cell ruptures to release them, a reproductive strategy never before seen in its group of organisms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How AI could make us work even harder
item.description: Technological progress has taken more than its fair share of the workload from humans over the years. Washing machines clean our clothes, tractors plow the fields and computers sort out administrative work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Permafrost melt could cost $261 billion in infrastructure damages, study suggests
item.description: A new study provides insight into the economic impact of melting permafrost on Arctic communities. Permafrost is ground that permanently remains below freezing for at least two consecutive years. Permafrost covers about 24% of the Northern Hemisphere, including large areas of Alaska, Canada and Siberia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: BESIII sets world's most stringent direct limit on Lambda hyperon electric dipole moment
item.description: The BESIII Collaboration, led by the Institute of High Energy Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, has achieved the world's most precise measurement of the electric dipole moment (EDM) of the Lambda (Λ) hyperon using quantum-entangled Λ–anti-Λ pairs produced in J/ψ decays. The result improves the experimental sensitivity by about three orders of magnitude compared with the previous measurement, providing a new way to probe charge-parity (CP) violation in particles containing strange quarks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pigment found in beets linked to plants' adaptation to harsh environments
item.description: The pigments that give beets their red color may have helped a major group of flowering plants repeatedly adapt to dry environments, setting the stage for the evolution of traits that allowed plants to adapt to some of the harshest environments on Earth, according to a University of Michigan study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum-optical spin glass could improve how AI remembers and learns
item.description: A new study has demonstrated that it is possible to make a network of atoms and photons that could improve how artificial intelligence stores and recalls memories. This network, called a quantum-optical spin glass, works as an associative memory, a form of AI that enables the recall of full memories from partial information—much like how humans can recognize a person's face in a blurred photograph. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2020, Ohio removed a dam from the once-polluted Cuyahoga River; it reopened 39 km of habitat
item.description: The removal of the Brecksville Diversion Dam has enhanced river habitats, allowing migrating fish to thrive. Researchers documented the arrival of fifteen new fish species within the lower Cuyahoga River. While native species have successfully reestablished their presence, the advent of nonnative species also marked a significant change in the ecosystem. Ongoing efforts to eliminate more dams aim to further rejuvenate the Cuyahoga River basin for future generations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Deep-sea methane filter develops faster than previously thought
item.description: A biological methane filter on the seafloor can form much faster than scientists previously believed. An international research team including a University of Bremen researcher observed this over six years at a newly formed methane seep in the deep sea. Earlier models assumed this process would take several decades. The study appears in National Science Review. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Metabolic networks provide clues about the earliest stages of enzyme evolution
item.description: The enzymes found in modern organisms are complex proteins, often with multiple folded substructures and specialized catalytic sites. Proteins are encoded by genes. Tracing the history of enzymes across all living organisms through gene comparisons leads to the last universal common ancestor (LUCA), a hypothetical organism that existed around 4 billion years ago and is believed to be the ancestor of life forms on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Neutron bone imaging brings T. rex to life
item.description: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest T. rex skeleton discovered, is helping scientists uncover new information about life on Earth 66 million years ago. Scotty's rib preserves something rarely seen in the fossil record: a healing injury frozen in time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: GenAI increasingly seen by investors as a key tool to research companies and evaluate stocks
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming integral to how retail investors research companies, with nearly half of those surveyed saying they have used it to process financial information or inform investment decisions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why doesn't Venus have a moon? A new study may have the answer
item.description: Venus is one of the solar system's most unusual planets. It may sometimes be called "Earth's twin" because of its similar size and density, but it rotates on its axis in the opposite direction of most planets, has surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead and lacks a moon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA to Cover Progress 96 Spacecraft Launch, Docking
item.description: NASA will provide live coverage of the launch and docking of a Roscosmos cargo spacecraft carrying about three tons of food, fuel, and supplies for the crew aboard the International Space Station. The unpiloted Progress 96 resupply spacecraft is scheduled to launch at 12:15 p.m. EDT (9:15 p.m. Baikonur time), Wednesday, Sept. 9, on a […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: First switchable graphene nanoribbon that twists on demand
item.description: Researchers at Nagoya University have built a graphene nanoribbon that can switch the direction of its twist using a natural solvent. Graphene nanoribbons are thin, ribbon-shaped structures made of fused carbon rings. Twisted or helical versions of these ribbons show promise for advanced light and electronic devices. However, until now, no graphene nanoribbon could switch its twist on demand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers develop precise new method to analyze secretions from individual salmon lice
item.description: A University of Stirling study could pave the way for more efficient study of the secretions that salmon lice use to avoid fish defenses, potentially enabling the development of new strategies to protect salmon from infestations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New enzyme mechanism explains how sulfur-reducing bacteria process elemental sulfur
item.description: Sulfur-reducing bacteria of the phylum Desulfobacterota play a crucial role in the global biogeochemical sulfur cycle. Species such as Geobacter sulfurreducens use elemental sulfur as a terminal electron acceptor during anaerobic respiration, producing sulfide that participates in the global sulfur cycle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Surf's up: How the seafloor shapes breaking waves
item.description: A new study led by surfing scientists at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego revealed the physical relationships underlying a pattern familiar to generations of surfers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A pair of spacecraft draw closer to Mercury after nearly decade-long voyage
item.description: Two Mercury-bound spacecraft left their mother ship behind on Thursday and headed down the home stretch of their nearly decade-long voyage to the solar system's smallest and closest-to-the-sun planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japanese scientist Shirakawa, co-winner of 2000 Nobel Prize in chemistry, dies at 90
item.description: Japanese scientist Hideki Shirakawa, co-winner of the 2000 Nobel Prize in chemistry for discovering and developing conductive polymers, has died. He was 90. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI suggests new physics experiments that could outperform human-designed setups
item.description: Research means asking questions of the universe. For centuries, clever minds have advanced science by devising ingenious experiments designed so their results reveal something about the laws of nature as clearly and unambiguously as possible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First-of-its-kind research balances the needs of solar farms and grazing
item.description: For insurers and operators alike, what grows under a solar array is almost as important as what sits on top of it. Grass height, moisture and biomass all influence how a site is insured, maintained and grazed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How stressed cells put the brakes on protein 'shipping'
item.description: Cells synthesize proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and these proteins are transported to the Golgi apparatus for distribution to their ultimate destinations inside and outside the cell. The structures that transport proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus are called COPII vesicles; the processes that regulate the formation of COPII vesicles are only partially understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacterial nanoplatform reprograms spleen immune cells to help prevent cancer recurrence
item.description: A research team led by Professor Yong Taik Lim at the SKKU Advanced Institute of Nanotechnology (SAINT), Sungkyunkwan University, have developed an engineered nanoplatform named t-SMC (trained immunity-mediated splenic myelopoiesis converter), which precisely targets the spleen to reverse splenic myelopoiesis toward an antitumoral immune phenotype. The research is published in the journal Advanced Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Viking South positioned to support industrial renewal in the Humber, report says
item.description: A study published today by the Geological Society and led by the University of Aberdeen concludes that the Viking South gas field has the geological suitability, proven containment integrity and operational readiness needed to become one of the UK's most advanced and reliable offshore carbon dioxide (CO₂) storage sites. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 4988-4994: More New Tricks for an Old Dog
item.description: Written by Michelle Minitti, MAHLI Deputy Principal Investigator Earth planning date: Friday, Aug. 21, 2026 After Curiosity’s 14 years on the surface, Mars continues to surprise. Both of our workspaces this week contained features unlike quite anything we have seen in the past — broad, shallow pits (like the one in the image above) dotted […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Microbial 'dark matter' yields 173 potential carbon dioxide-fixing strains
item.description: There are millions of species of bacteria and archaea on Earth, remarkably little is known about most of them. Now, researchers have mined the genomes of thousands of microorganisms preserved at the RIKEN BioResource Research Center (BRC) to find organisms that may be capable of capturing CO2. BRC, located in Tsukuba—one of Japan's largest centers of scientific research—is a unique, world-class research facility. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How underwater 'booms' could provide earlier warning of deadly volcanic tsunamis
item.description: The massive January 2022 eruption of Hunga volcano in the Kingdom of Tonga took the world by surprise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gharial pop patterns and gecko calls uncover reptiles' overlooked social communication
item.description: Along the sandy banks of northern India's Chambal River, crocodile-like gharials glide silently through the water—but if a gharial spots a stranger, the quiet may be punctuated by a series of explosive pops. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists solve years-long mystery of 'beating' signal in a quantum material
item.description: A team of Korean researchers has become the first in the world to identify the origin of the "beating" signal that has long been a major obstacle to interpreting quantum signals in topological insulator (TI) nanowires. Their analysis confirmed that the beating arises when two different quantum oscillations overlap: one created by topological electronic states on the surface and the other by ordinary electronic states inside the nanowire. This achievement provides a key criterion for interpreting the signals of topological quantum devices and realizing desired electronic states. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shellharbour families call for youth spaces, mental health support and affordable activities
item.description: New research by the University of Wollongong's (UOW) Early Start, commissioned by Barnardos Australia's Communities for Children Shellharbour program and released this week (Thursday, Sept. 3), set out to answer a simple but powerful question: What do young people and families in the Shellharbour region need to thrive? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warming peatlands can turn them from carbon sinks to leaks
item.description: Peatlands, which store significant global soil carbon, are now releasing it. Warming temperatures cause these ecosystems to shift from carbon accumulators to emitters. This transition occurs rapidly, even with modest warming of four degrees Fahrenheit. Researchers observed carbon loss rates significantly faster than historical accumulation rates. These findings impact global climate forecasting models and future predictions. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Igniting Roman’s Journey
item.description: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Roman pairs a large […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gary Daines

item.title: Can Australian businesses legally ban customers from using smart glasses?
item.description: Businesses and local councils around Australia are increasingly imposing their own restrictions on "smart glasses," responding to customers' concerns about being covertly recorded in public places. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dual-purpose qubit design could speed operations while cutting quantum errors
item.description: Researchers from MIT have designed a new qubit architecture that enables qubits to interact with each other much more quickly while remaining very stable. This advance could someday help scientists build practical quantum computers that can run long, complex algorithms with high accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat has a memory—and a new theoretical framework can track it
item.description: Heat, it turns out, has a memory. A cooling cup of coffee may not seem particularly thoughtful. At the scale of a kitchen, heat appears to follow a straightforward rule: it moves from warmer places to cooler ones. Leave the cup unattended long enough, and the disappointing result offers convincing evidence that this rule works. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First DDT, now the flu: Peregrine falcons in San Francisco Bay Area hit hard by H5N1 variant
item.description: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) featured prominently in the news during 2020 as it took the lives of millions of birds across the globe. While the worst seems to be behind us, population-level effects are just now emerging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who hears you say 'thank you?' It matters more than you might think
item.description: There are many ways to say thank you. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum control algorithm looks to explain how birds migrate
item.description: The hidden world of quantum mechanics exists at scales many orders of magnitude smaller than living organisms, yet scientists have long theorized that quantum effects play an important role in biology. Birds' ability to sense magnetic fields during migration is one of the best-known mysteries in this field, with leading theories suggesting that this sensing could be achieved by exploiting quantum entanglement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why feeding birds can make you feel better
item.description: More than 56 million U.S. adults feed wild birds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Superbubble Scene
item.description: This Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista called N44. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Ancient “living fossils” may reveal how complex life began
item.description: A newly discovered microbe living inside ancient stromatolite communities may offer a rare look at how complex life first emerged. Researchers captured the first direct images of an Asgard archaeon physically connected to a bacterium, with the two microbes appearing to exchange nutrients and other compounds. Scientists think similar partnerships billions of years ago may have helped produce the first complex cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Overqualification can make or break family life, study reveals
item.description: New research shows overqualified employees who prioritize work over family are more likely to let anxiety and fear about their careers spill into their home lives, creating damaging conflict. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA scientists discover a giant 10-sided pattern on Saturn
item.description: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Can an AI tutor help students improve at math?
item.description: As schools contend with rapid developments in artificial intelligence, new research from the University of Toronto Mississauga suggests an AI tutor could help students with math, but only if it holds back answers and coaches them through problems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When panic freezes people: Virtual quake tests capture real-time fear and injury risk
item.description: Growing up, many of us were taught to drop, cover and hold on during an earthquake. The guidance is straightforward, but how people actually respond when the ground starts shaking can be far more complicated. Now, UC Berkeley researchers are studying what happens in those critical moments and how fear and risk perception influence people's actions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1999, scientists dropped 45 tons of wollastonite over a 29-acre New Hampshire watershed
item.description: In an ambitious forest restoration initiative in New Hampshire, researchers sought to mitigate the effects of acid rain. They introduced calcium-rich minerals, leading to an initial boost in tree vitality and growth. However, this solution inadvertently resulted in a staggering increase in nitrogen levels in nearby streams, releasing thirty times more inorganic nitrogen compared to untreated regions. This outcome underscores the intricate dynamics of ecosystems in response to human intervention. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: The biggest black hole merger ever observed could be less massive than it appears
item.description: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime created when pairs of black holes spiral into each other and eventually merge. But if this ripple has been warped by another massive object on its way to Earth, a new analysis suggests that these black holes might appear far larger than they really are. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Our pay is called a 'salary,' but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?
item.description: Every other Wednesday, like clockwork, my salary arrives in my bank account. By Thursday, most of it is gone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists just overturned a century-old physics assumption
item.description: Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University have discovered an unexpected form of the Hall effect, overturning the long-held assumption that this electrical response only appears when a magnetic field points perpendicular to a material. Beyond expanding a century-old principle of physics, the finding could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors for electronics, transportation, and medical technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Looking back to forecast the future of lobster
item.description: For generations, the lobster fishery has been central to the cultural and economic identity of Maine and Atlantic Canada. Predicting what the future holds for the species—and the people who depend on it—has long been a priority for scientists and resource managers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
item.description: Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Salt may have helped turn Earth into a frozen world 700 million years ago
item.description: Earth may have been pushed deeper into a global deep freeze by something surprisingly ordinary: salt. Around 700 million years ago, Earth entered periods of extreme glaciation known as Snowball Earth, when ice is thought to have spread across much or potentially all of the planet's surface. Scientists have long known that expanding ice could have helped drive this transition: As bright ice replaces darker ocean water, more sunlight is reflected back into space, causing the planet to cool further and allowing even more ice to form. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Teenage kicks: Why Australian youth culture must be preserved
item.description: From the rock 'n' roll and punk scenes, soda fountains and graduation-week celebrations, surfers, skaters, ravers and the modern-day Eshay, generations of young Australians have been creating culture, but much of it risks disappearing from the historical record. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Informal supporters share experiences of NDIS behavior support practitioners
item.description: A new national survey of informal supporters of people with disabilities who have received NDIS-funded behavior support services has identified wide variation in supporters' confidence in practitioners' knowledge and skills, pointing to a need for greater transparency about practitioner expertise and stronger, more consistent, rights-based behavior support across the NDIS. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why Britons disagree about poverty: They draw the line differently
item.description: People with different political beliefs do not only disagree about how much poverty exists in Britain but they also differ over whether the same material circumstances should be defined as poverty, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
item.description: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Los últimos mensajes de la pareja italiana que mató a su hija discapacitada y luego se suicidó: "Escribamos en el grupo y nos echamos unas risas"
item.description: Los forenses practican las autopsias y el test de la parafina a la pareja hallada muerta junto a su hija de cinco años en Roma, mientras los investigadores intentan esclarecer la mecánica exacta del crimen a partir de la pistola Glock incautada en la vivienda Leer Fuente: El Mundo - Internacional.

item.title: Latest updates: BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury
item.description: After eight years of travelling through the inner Solar System, BepiColombo is arriving at Mercury. This page will show the latest updates throughout the mission's arrival. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Electron spin unlocks magnetic control of hydrogen surface reactions
item.description: Chemical reactions at surfaces play a central role in many processes, including catalysis and materials synthesis. It is well known that the outcome of these reactions is influenced by the translational, vibrational and rotational motions of atoms and molecules. Now, a study shows that electron spin, another fundamental property of matter, also influences how chemical reactions at surfaces unfold. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heavy water's atmospheric fingerprints boost weather forecasts for up to five days
item.description: Weather forecasts rely on many different kinds of data, including temperature, humidity and wind. For the first time, researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, have demonstrated that a long-theorized improvement to weather models—adding data on water isotopes in the atmosphere—does work. They showed that incorporating satellite measurements of water vapor isotopes into weather models improves forecasts of atmospheric conditions for up to five days, including predictions of heavy rainfall in many regions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2010, US scientists tracked dye 41.2 miles in Montana’s Missouri River; a reservoir held it 8.2 hours
item.description: Scientists conducted a dye-tracing experiment on Montana's Missouri River. This study examined how substances move through the waterway over forty miles. The dye traveled at different speeds through various river sections and reservoirs. Researchers measured how the dye plume spread along the river's direction. This data aids in predicting contaminant movement and planning for accidental spills. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: AI boom is testing tech firms' climate pledges
item.description: Technology companies are stepping up their climate commitments but not fast enough to counter rapidly growing energy needs linked to the artificial intelligence boom, a report said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Chile, injured penguins sport copper vests to help them heal
item.description: Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins—snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Underwater meadows sustain millions in extreme poverty
item.description: A study provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that seagrass meadows act as a critical safety net for millions of coastal people living in extreme poverty across the Indo-Pacific. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta de Artemis II: “La respuesta a nuestra misión aquí en la Tierra superó con creces todo lo que habíamos imaginado y esperado”
item.description: Tras su regreso a la Tierra, Donald Trump le entregó a cada tripulante una medalla Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso, durante una ceremonia en el Centro Espacial Jonhson de Houston Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
item.description: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: September brings a dazzling Venus and a glowing Harvest Moon
item.description: September’s sky features brilliant Venus, the Milky Way’s hazy center, and the seasonal turning point of the equinox. The month ends with a glowing Harvest Moon rising near Saturn and faint Neptune. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La mala noticia es que el oxígeno de la Tierra tiene fecha de caducidad. La buena es que no estaremos aquí para verlo
item.description: Podemos respirar tranquilos. También los nietos de los nietos de nuestros nietos. Pero el oxígeno que sustenta la vida compleja en la Tierra no será eterno. A nuestra atmósfera rica en oxígeno le quedan, aproximadamente, mil millones de años . Entonces, el cambio será drástico. Una desoxigenación rápida. Un estudio internacional publicado en Nature Geoscience detalla los cálculos. Después de hacer más de 400.000 simulaciones sobre la evolución geológica y biológica de nuestro planeta, científicos japoneses y estadounidenses llegaron a la conclusión de que la Tierra experimentará una… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
item.description: Fighting escalated in the Middle East over the weekend after US airstrikes on Sunday targeted Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak. The exchange of fire was instigated by the US in retaliation against Iran’s new capabilities for firing mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s use of rocket launchers to deploy sea mines into the strategic waterway would be unprecedented, but not implausible. Even so, some analysts remain sceptical. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Sébastian SEIBT

item.title: Hong Kong considers DNA testing amid concerns over ‘fighting dog’ classification
item.description: Hong Kong authorities are considering genetic testing as a supplementary tool for identifying breeds, an official has said after enforcement action against suspected fighting dogs sparked public concern. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) also said on Thursday that owners could keep existing fighting dogs, provided they complied with statutory requirements, and urged owners not to abandon their pets. Dr Michelle Yeung Lee, the department’s principal veterinary officer,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Leopold Chen

item.title: Biodegradable 'nanobone' could one day help regrow bone without painful grafts
item.description: For children born with cleft lip and palate, repairing gaps in the jawbone often means waiting until they are 10 to 12 years old before undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. University of Sydney researchers have developed a biodegradable "nanobone" material that allows the body to harness its own healing properties to regrow bone, offering a potential future alternative to procedures that have changed little in more than 50 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: With education technology, engagement is not the same as learning
item.description: A new report from the American Psychological Association warns that student engagement with educational technology is not the same as learning—and that generative AI tools pose particular risks by improving students' immediate performance without building their underlying knowledge or skills. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ADHD may have a surprising creative advantage
item.description: Some of the attention patterns that make ADHD challenging may also help spark creativity by allowing the brain to explore more ideas and unexpected connections. Researchers think creative activities could potentially channel this “defocused attention” while helping strengthen the brain systems involved in focus and self-control. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study reveals distinct patterns across single-, multi-, and mass homicides
item.description: An updated analysis of U.S. homicide data has found that intimate partner violence (IPV) often precipitates mass homicide and is also frequently associated with multi-victim and single-victim deaths. The study categorizes homicides into single-victim, multi-victim (2–3 victims) and mass (4 or more victims, excluding the perpetrator) fatalities, revealing distinct demographics and circumstances. The findings of the study published in Annals of Epidemiology, can help inform the development of tailored strategies to prevent homicide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Each extra hour of prolonged sitting linked to 9% higher cancer death risk
item.description: Sitting for long, uninterrupted stretches may carry greater health risks than sitting the same amount of time in shorter bouts. Researchers found that each extra hour of prolonged sedentary behavior was associated with a 9% higher risk of cancer death. Breaking up sitting with movement showed the opposite pattern, while replacing an hour of prolonged sitting with light activity was linked to a 12% lower risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Crash in dugong population estimates, a warning sign governments can't ignore
item.description: A 50% decline in the Gulf of Carpentaria dugong population estimate is a wake-up call for urgent action to protect dugongs in the Gulf, based on surveys undertaken by researchers from James Cook University, Charles Darwin University and Indigenous Ranger groups. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China launches largest-ever academic misconduct crackdown after ‘Student Geng’ scrutiny
item.description: Four Chinese academics who lost posts at leading universities after a high-profile blogger flagged their research for misconduct have come under official investigation by China’s leading funder of basic research. The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) published details on August 26 of 31 new misconduct cases at universities and hospitals across China, involving more than 40 researchers – its largest such public disclosure to date. Among them were four prominent professors... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
